prompt.context: Our client is an Italian online apparel store called 7SHIRTS. The company sells casual pants, polo shirts, sweaters, but it is famous for its unique trendy patterned shirts. The value proposition is to have the perfect shirt for each day of the week. The company has experienced strong growth in the last two years but profitability has declined in the last year. The CEO has hired us to understand the reason for the decline and to receive suggestions on how to improve profitability.
prompt.question: What is driving the decline in profitability and how would you improve it?

clarifying_info.q: What is the company's revenue and how has it grown?
clarifying_info.a: The company has a turnover of about €1.5M with a growth of 20% in the last two years. Net profit is still positive but went down by 21% in 2020 after a stable growth period.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a specific profitability target to reach?
clarifying_info.a: There is no specific profitability goal.

clarifying_info.q: Does the company manufacture its own products?
clarifying_info.a: The company does not manufacture products directly. It buys them from a supplier and sells them online under its own 7SHIRTS brand.

clarifying_info.q: In which markets does the company operate?
clarifying_info.a: The company sells in five European countries: Italy, France, Spain, UK, and Germany.

exhibits.title: Revenue by Product (2017–2020)
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart showing annual revenue from 2017 to 2020, broken down by product category: Polo Shirts, Casual Pants, Sweaters, and Shirts. Total revenue grows each year up to approximately €1.6M in 2020.

exhibits.title: Costs Variation YoY and Marketing Budget by Product
exhibits.shows: Two tables: (1) year-over-year cost variation percentages by cost line (COGS, Shipping, Marketing, Salary, Other) from 2017 to 2020; (2) marketing budget allocation by product and margin by product.

exhibits.title: Marketing Tool Performance in 2020
exhibits.shows: A table comparing four marketing channels (Facebook, Google Ads, Newsletter, Affiliate Marketing) across spend, unique visitors, conversion rate, and average order value. Additional data on average purchases per year and average customer relationship length are provided.

framework: Revenue side: volume (units sold) x price; product mix shift toward shirts
Cost side: COGS, Shipping, Marketing, Salary, Other
Identify fastest-growing cost lines from Exhibit 2 (COGS +33%, Marketing +30% YoY in 2020)
Link marketing budget concentration (95% on shirts) to product mix shift
Analyze marketing channel efficiency: calculate CLTV vs. cost per customer for each channel
Identify unprofitable channels and recommend reallocation

questions.prompt: Walk through the profitability tree and identify which cost lines are driving the decline.
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure costs as COGS, Shipping, Marketing, Salary, and Other. From Exhibit 2, COGS and Marketing show the largest YoY increases in 2020 (+33% and +30% respectively). Shipping, Salary, and Other are relatively stable. The candidate should flag COGS and Marketing as the primary drivers and probe what is causing each.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2, explain why COGS has increased so sharply.
questions.guidance: Exhibit 1 shows revenue mix shifting significantly toward Shirts over 2017–2020. Exhibit 2 shows that Shirts have the lowest margin (65%) versus Polo Shirts (80%), Casual Pants (80%), and Sweaters (85%). Simultaneously, 95% of the marketing budget is allocated to Shirts. The marketing push on the lowest-margin product has driven a product mix shift that raises blended COGS as a percentage of revenue.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, calculate the profitability of each marketing channel by computing Customer Lifetime Value (CLTV) and cost per customer acquired.
questions.guidance: Candidate should set up the formulas correctly: Total purchases over lifetime = avg_relationship_years × avg_purchases_per_year = 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 purchases. CLTV = avg_order_value × 1.5. Cost per customer = total_spend / (unique_visitors × conversion_rate). Profit per customer = CLTV − cost per customer. Facebook is the only unprofitable channel (−€10 per customer). The candidate should recommend reducing or fixing Facebook spend.

math.setup: Total lifetime purchases = 3 years × 0.5 purchases/year = 1.5 purchases. CLTV = avg_order_value × 1.5. Cost per customer = total_spend / (unique_visitors × conversion_rate).
steps: Facebook: CLTV = 60 × 1.5 = €90. Customers acquired = 150,000 × 1% = 1,500. Cost per customer = 150,000 / 1,500 = €100. Profit = 90 − 100 = −€10 (LOSS).
Google Ads: CLTV = 60 × 1.5 = €90. Customers = 50,000 × 2% = 1,000. Cost per customer = 30,000 / 1,000 = €30. Profit = 90 − 30 = €60.
Newsletter: CLTV = 70 × 1.5 = €105. Customers = 100,000 × 2% = 2,000. Cost per customer = 20,000 / 2,000 = €10. Profit = 105 − 10 = €95.
Affiliate Marketing: CLTV = 60 × 1.5 = €90. Customers = 70,000 × 3% = 2,100. Cost per customer = 42,000 / 2,100 = €20. Profit = 90 − 20 = €70.
math.answer: Facebook: −€10/customer (unprofitable). Google Ads: +€60. Newsletter: +€95. Affiliate Marketing: +€70. Facebook is the only channel destroying value.

brainstorming.prompt: How would you improve the profitability of the Facebook marketing tool? Also, what are possible reasons why Facebook is not profitable?

categories.name: Improve Facebook efficiency – funnel levers
ideas: Increase unique visitors while maintaining cost per click: change targeting geography, demographics, or product category (e.g., shift to sweaters or casual pants with higher margins)
Improve conversion rate: test new ad copy, new creative imagery, refine audience targeting
Increase average order value: cross-sell, push higher-priced items, improve landing pages
Increase CLTV: launch loyalty programmes, improve repurchase frequency, lengthen customer relationship

categories.name: External reasons Facebook underperforms
ideas: Stronger competitors bidding up cost per conversion on Facebook
Macroeconomic conditions reducing purchase intent on social media
Shift in consumer behaviour away from Facebook (especially younger demographics)

categories.name: Internal reasons Facebook underperforms
ideas: Products advertised are not appealing in Facebook context
Incorrect ad content or creative execution

recommendation: 7SHIRTS' profitability decline is driven by two linked issues: (1) 95% of the marketing budget is concentrated on Shirts, the lowest-margin product (65% vs. 80–85% for other categories), causing a product mix shift that inflates COGS; and (2) Facebook, which absorbs the largest marketing spend (€150K), generates a loss of €10 per customer acquired.

Immediate actions: reduce or reallocate Facebook budget to Newsletter (€95 profit/customer) and Affiliate Marketing (€70 profit/customer), which are the most efficient channels. Rebalance the marketing budget to promote higher-margin products (Sweaters, Casual Pants, Polo Shirts) alongside Shirts to improve blended margin.

Longer-term: if Facebook is retained, redesign campaigns with different audience targeting, creative, and product focus. Use cross-selling tactics on all channels to increase average order value. Consider loyalty programmes to extend customer lifetime.
risks: Shifting budget away from Facebook may reduce total customer acquisition volume in the short term
Reallocating budget to other channels does not guarantee the same conversion economics if competitors increase spend there
Reducing emphasis on Shirts could dilute the core brand identity ('perfect shirt for every day of the week')
next_steps: Analyse main competitors' digital marketing strategies and spend
Run A/B tests on Facebook with different audiences, creatives, and product mixes before fully cutting the channel
Explore emerging platforms (e.g., TikTok for Business) to diversify acquisition
Analyse customer behaviour data to identify upsell and cross-sell opportunities across product lines
